newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Thailand sees higher sugar output, eyes MidEast.
newsitem.headline: Thailand sees higher sugar output, eyes MidEast.

text.p: Thailand's sugar output was expected to increase in the 1997/1998 season, after a dip in the current season, Pramode Vidtayasuk, cane and sugar board secretary general said on Wednesday.
But the size of the sugar cane crop in the new season, which kicks off in November, was seen capped at 60 million tonnes, he told Reuters in an interview at a sugar meeting in Mauritius.
"Some people have already started planting. In terms of cane production, it will be increased... but it will not exceed 60 million tonnes," he said.
Thailand's 1996/97 sugar crushing season had finished early this year following a drop in cane production on the back of poor weather conditions, Vidtayasuk said.
"Last year we had about 57.7 million tonnes (of crushed cane), but this year it is around 56.2," he said.
Latest official estimates show sugar production so far for this season at 5.795 million tonnes compared with a total of 6.026 million tonnes in the previous crop year.
Vidtayasuk said Thailand had no immediate plans to expand its crushing capacity.
"We see no point in expanding our crushing capacity at this moment... We think the capacity of our production is still enough for 60-62 million tonnes."

Vidtayasuk said although Thailand's major export market remained the East, it had found some new export destinations in the Middle East during 1996 and expanded some existing ones. Quantities, however, remained small, he said.
"Altogether (for the Middle East) it was about 200,000 tonnes in 1996, about half white and half raw.
"Jordan started importing sugar from Thailand in 1996 for the very first time. UAE imported raw sugar, 70,000 tonnes, for the first time."
Iran was also a new buyer of raw sugar in 1996. It has previously bought white from Thailand.
Vidtayasuk said there was a 10-fold increase in exports to Yemen from 8,000 tonnes in 1995 to 84,000. White sugar to the UAE had increased almost three-fold to 56,000 tonnes.
"But we sold less white sugar to Saudi Arabia than the year before," he said.
